text: Why do we sometimes use A, and sometimes THE?
For the answer, let’s visit England a thousand years ago!
In 1066, the king of England dies without an heir.
Now England needs a king:
England needs a king.
But three men each want the throne!
First, Harold is crowned.
But the king of Norway invades!
Harold defeats him,
but before he can catch his breath,
William arrives with another army!
This time, Harold is killed, and William becomes:
The king of England!
Notice what happened?
First, we said A KING:
a king—
we haven’t specified which one.
But THE KING means that particular king!
The roots of this distinction go back to Old English!
A comes from ĀN, meaning “one.”
THE belongs to the demonstrative family, like “that”:
something like “that one” or “the very one.”
So what’s the key difference?
When your listener can identify exactly which thing you mean,
we usually use THE;
even if it hasn’t been mentioned before!
